title: NiTi Composites Reinforced with TiC: Influence of the Chosen Incorporation Strategy
content: Advanced materials with high kinetic energy dissipation, crucial for ballistic protection of personnel and machinery, are driving innovation in the field. Modern ballistic protection research focuses on weight reduction, energy dissipation, and impact resistance, achieved through novel material combinations and innovative approaches. Standard ballistic armor consists of a steel, Al- or Ti-alloy backplate, intermediate ceramic tiles (SiC, Al2O3, or B₄C), and a fiber-reinforced polymer front plate. The first two layers fragment and slow projectiles, while the backplate absorbs ∼40% of the impact energy [1, 2]. However, at high-velocity impacts, ceramic layers degrade, compromising protection. Long-term cohesion of these layers is also critical, especially in extreme conditions. A promising strategy replaces polymers with metal matrices embedding ceramic particles via functionally graded layers. Additionally, integrating 1D (CNTs) and 2D (graphene) carbon structures—known for their exceptional strength (200 GPa and 130 GPa) and elastic moduli (≥1 TPa) [3], could surpass modern polymer composites. Optimizing material parameters to create nanostructured composites from carbides and carbon-based structures, rather than waste by-products, further enhances research potential.
